stem: A healthy 2-month-old boy receives an oral live attenuated poliovirus vaccine. His father, who lives in the home and changes diapers, is receiving chemotherapy for lymphoma and has profound immunosuppression. The vaccine virus is shed in the infant's stool for several weeks.
oneliner: 2-month-old healthy boy + oral live poliovirus vaccine + virus shed in stool + father on chemotherapy changes diapers → what complication can follow?
ask: Which complication can follow in the household?

options.A: Serum sickness in the infant 1 to 2 weeks later
options.C: Paralytic poliomyelitis from the vaccine strain in the immunosuppressed father
options.D: No risk, because the vaccine strain is attenuated
options.E: Arthus reaction at the infant's injection site

whyNot.A: **Serum sickness** follows foreign serum or drugs, not an oral live vaccine
whyNot.B: **Anaphylaxis** needs prior IgE sensitization to a vaccine component
whyNot.D: The strain is attenuated but can **revert and cause disease in the immunosuppressed**
whyNot.E: An **Arthus reaction** follows injection, not an oral vaccine, in an already sensitized host

answer: Vaccine-strain poliomyelitis in the immunocompromised contact
why: A **live attenuated** strain **replicates in the gut** and is **shed**. In an **immunocompromised** contact it can **cause disease**, such as paralytic polio, because there is no immune check. Such patients should avoid live vaccine, and contacts get the **inactivated** form.
chain: Live attenuated vaccine replicates in the infant
Virus shed in stool
Father is exposed via the fecal-oral route
Weak immunity cannot control the strain
Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis

idea.rule: Live vaccines can infect people with weak immunity, so they and their contacts need non-live options.
also: Live vaccines: MMR, varicella, rotavirus, oral polio, yellow fever, intranasal flu
Avoid live vaccines in pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency
Inactivated polio vaccine is the one used in the United States
Rotavirus vaccine strain can be shed in infant stool

stem: A 25-year-old woman was treated with a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin for secondary syphilis, when she had a rash on her palms and soles. Her RPR titer was 1:64. She returns at 6 and 12 months for follow-up, and both RPR and a treponemal antibody test are repeated.
oneliner: 25F + treated secondary syphilis with benzathine penicillin + RPR 1:64 + follow-up at 6 and 12 months → what happens to each test?
ask: Which pattern of results is expected at 12 months?

options.A: RPR stays positive for life, FTA-ABS turns negative
options.B: RPR titer falls, while the treponemal test stays positive
options.C: Both tests turn negative within 2 weeks
options.E: RPR rises as a sign of cure

whyNot.A: That is **backwards**: it is the **treponemal test** that persists
whyNot.C: Treponemal antibody does not vanish; it **stays positive** for life, and neither test clears in 2 weeks
whyNot.D: The **RPR** is expected to fall with treatment, so it does **not stay unchanged**
whyNot.E: A **rising** RPR means treatment failure or reinfection, not cure

answer: RPR titer falls; FTA-ABS stays positive
why: The **RPR/VDRL** measures **antibody to cardiolipin** released from damaged cells; its titer **falls with effective treatment** (fourfold drop) and is used to follow response. **Treponemal tests** (FTA-ABS, TPPA) usually stay **positive for life**.
chain: Penicillin kills Treponema pallidum
Tissue damage and cardiolipin release fall
Anticardiolipin RPR titer drops
Treponemal antibody persists
RPR for follow-up, FTA-ABS stays positive

idea.rule: Nontreponemal tests follow activity; treponemal tests record exposure.
also: RPR/VDRL false positives: lupus, antiphospholipid syndrome, pregnancy, viral infection
A fourfold fall in titer shows response
Rising titer means failure or reinfection
Prozone phenomenon can cause a false-negative RPR

stem: A 33-year-old woman with HIV infection, who stopped her medications months ago, has had 2 weeks of headache and a seizure this morning. She is afebrile and alert, with mild right arm weakness and a supple neck. Her CD4 count is 22/mm3. MRI shows two ring-enhancing lesions in the left cerebral cortex with surrounding edema. Serum anti-Toxoplasma IgG is positive. She is started on pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and leucovorin.
oneliner: 33F + HIV with CD4 22 + headache + seizure + mild right arm weakness + supple neck + 2 ring-enhancing cortical lesions + positive Toxoplasma IgG + started on pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine → repeat MRI at 2 weeks?
ask: Which of the following is most likely to be seen on repeat MRI 2 weeks later?

options.A: Larger lesions spreading along the ventricular lining
options.B: New nonenhancing lesions in the white matter
options.C: Smaller lesions with less surrounding edema
options.D: Unchanged lesions with new meningeal enhancement
options.E: Cystic lesions each containing a visible scolex

whyNot.A: Growth despite treatment points to **lymphoma** and calls for biopsy; **two cortical lesions with positive Toxoplasma IgG** predict a response
whyNot.B: Describes PML, whose lesions do not enhance or cause edema; hers are **ring-enhancing with edema**
whyNot.D: Meningeal enhancement suggests cryptococcal or tuberculous meningitis; she has a **supple neck** and **parenchymal ring lesions**
whyNot.E: A scolex marks neurocysticercosis; **positive Toxoplasma IgG with CD4 22** and ring lesions point to toxoplasmosis

answer: Lesions shrink with less edema, confirming cerebral toxoplasmosis
why: **CD4 below 100**, multiple **ring-enhancing lesions** and **positive Toxoplasma IgG** mean reactivated cerebral toxoplasmosis. Empiric **pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine** usually shrinks the lesions within about 2 weeks, and that response confirms the diagnosis; a lesion that grows needs biopsy for **CNS lymphoma**.
chain: CD4 falls below 100 and latent tissue cysts reactivate
Parasites multiply and cause necrotizing abscesses
Ring-enhancing lesions with edema cause seizure and weakness
Empiric pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine (with leucovorin) is started
Lesions shrink by about 2 weeks, confirming the diagnosis without biopsy

idea.rule: In AIDS with CD4 below 100, ring-enhancing lesions and positive IgG, treat toxoplasmosis empirically and let the response be the test.
also: Primary CNS lymphoma: usually one periventricular lesion, EBV in CSF; biopsy if no response to treatment
TMP-SMX prophylaxis starts when CD4 falls below 100 in Toxoplasma IgG-positive patients
Leucovorin is added to prevent pyrimethamine marrow suppression
Sulfa-allergic patients receive clindamycin with pyrimethamine

stem: A 32-year-old man was bitten on the hand by a puppy that later died. Three weeks later he has tingling at the healed bite site, followed by agitation and disorientation. He had no treatment after the bite.
oneliner: 32M + puppy bite 3 weeks ago, animal later died + tingling at healed bite site + agitation, disorientation + no post-exposure treatment → what happens next?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely course?

options.C: Chronic latent infection with periodic reactivations

whyNot.A: Once **encephalitis symptoms appear**, rabies is almost always fatal and does not resolve in 2 weeks
whyNot.C: Latency with reactivation is a **herpesvirus** pattern; rabies is not latent
whyNot.D: Flaccid paralysis with recovery describes **poliomyelitis**; rabies progresses to death
whyNot.E: Acyclovir treats **herpes viruses** and has no effect on the rabies virus

why: **Paresthesia at the bite site followed by agitation** shows rabies virus has reached the CNS. After **symptoms start**, rabies is **almost uniformly fatal**, so prevention (**wound care, immune globulin and vaccine**) must come before symptoms.
chain: Bite introduces virus
Virus travels along peripheral nerve
Paresthesia at the bite site
Encephalitis with agitation
Coma and death

idea.rule: Rabies is preventable after exposure but almost always fatal once symptoms begin.
also: Post-exposure: wound washing, immune globulin, vaccine
